content: The actinoid series, as defined by IUPAC terminology, consists of 15 chemical elements with atomic numbers ranging from 89 (actinium) to 103 (lawrencium) on the periodic table. The name actinoid is derived from the first element in the series, actinium, which itself originates from the Greek word aktis, meaning ray, reflecting the radioactive nature of these elements. IUPAC recommends the term actinoid over actinide because the suffix -ide typically denotes ions, whereas -oid implies similarity to actinium. Additionally, the Latin root of -ide translates to sons of actinium, while -oid means similar to actinium. The actinoid series is sometimes included in definitions of rare earth elements. However, alternative arrangements of the periodic table may exclude actinium or lawrencium from being grouped with the other actinoids. Unlike the lanthanoid series, the actinoids exhibit less uniformity in their chemical properties and display a broader range of oxidation states. This variability initially caused confusion about whether actinium, thorium, and uranium should be classified as d-block elements. All actinoids are radioactive, but only thorium and uranium occur naturally in the Earth's crust in significant quantities. Neptunium and plutonium can appear naturally in trace amounts within uranium ores due to decay or bombardment processes. The remaining actinoids were either discovered in nuclear fallout or synthesized in particle accelerators. The latter half of the series is characterized by extremely short half-lives. In the periodic table, actinoids are typically placed below the main body, beneath the lanthanoid series, in a footnote-like arrangement. A full-width version of the periodic table more clearly displays the position of the actinoids. Organometallic compounds containing actinoids are referred to as organoactinoids. Historically, the chemical properties of actinium (89) through uranium (92) suggested a relationship to the transition metals, leading to the assumption that transuranium elements would share similar characteristics. However, during his Manhattan Project research in 1944, Glenn T. Seaborg encountered unexpected difficulties isolating americium (95) and curium (96). This led him to hypothesize that these elements might belong to a different series rather than the transition metals, which would explain their distinct chemical properties. In 1945, despite opposition from colleagues, Seaborg proposed a groundbreaking revision to Mendeleev's periodic table: the actinide series. He published his actinide concept that year, predicting that the actinoids would form a transition series analogous to the lanthanoid series of rare earth elements. In 1961, Antoni Przybylski discovered a star containing unusually high concentrations of actinoids, further highlighting the significance of this series.
